pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny soft insects that cluster on stems and new growth. Aphids love nasturtiums, which is exactly why gardeners use the plant as a trap to lure them away from vegetables. On a plant you are keeping, hose them off or use insecticidal soap; the flowers also draw ladybugs and hoverflies that eat them.
pests.note_seasoned: Expected, and by design: aphids strongly prefer nasturtium, which is the basis of its trap-crop use. On a trap stand, monitor and pull or destroy the planting once it is heavily loaded. On an ornamental or edible planting, dislodge with water sprays or insecticidal soap; resident hoverflies, lacewings, and ladybugs the flowers attract usually keep numbers in check.

pests.name: Cabbage white caterpillars (imported cabbageworm)
pests.note_beginner: Green caterpillars, the larvae of the white cabbage butterfly, that chew holes in nasturtium leaves. Pick them off by hand, or use the natural spray Bt if they get bad.
pests.note_seasoned: Larvae of the imported cabbage white (Pieris rapae) feed on nasturtium foliage, which shares the mustard-oil chemistry of brassicas. Hand-pick, exclude with row cover where practical, or treat with Bt for heavy pressure. Caterpillar holes on edible leaves are cosmetic; harvest clean young leaves.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.note_beginner: Tiny black beetles that hop and chew small round holes in the leaves. Nasturtiums actually draw flea beetles, so like aphids they can be used to pull these pests off more valuable crops.
pests.note_seasoned: Small jumping beetles that pit the foliage with shot-holes; nasturtium is among the plants flea beetles favor, so it doubles as a flea-beetle trap. Damage is mostly cosmetic on an established plant. Floating row cover protects young plantings; pick young leaves from below the worst feeding for the kitchen.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.note_beginner: These chew ragged holes in leaves and young plants in damp weather, and tender nasturtium seedlings are a favorite. Hand-pick at night, remove hiding spots, or use iron-phosphate bait.
pests.note_seasoned: Ragged feeding on seedlings and low, sprawling foliage in damp conditions; the trailing mat of a vigorous nasturtium offers harborage. Reduce mulch and debris, hand-pick at night, or use iron-phosphate bait.

pests.name: Whiteflies and spider mites
pests.note_beginner: Tiny insects on the undersides of leaves: whiteflies fly up in a cloud when disturbed, and spider mites cause fine speckling in hot, dry spells. Spray with water or insecticidal soap if they build up.
pests.note_seasoned: Whiteflies and, in hot dry conditions, spider mites colonize leaf undersides on stressed or sheltered plants. Hose foliage, raise humidity with base watering, and use insecticidal soap for persistent infestations; both are secondary pests rarely needing intervention outdoors.

diseases.name: Mosaic and aphid-borne viruses
diseases.note_beginner: Viruses spread by aphids can mottle, streak, or distort the leaves. There is no cure, so pull and discard badly affected plants and keep aphids in check.
diseases.note_seasoned: Several viruses, mostly aphid-vectored, cause mosaic mottling, ringspots, and leaf distortion. There is no treatment; rogue out symptomatic plants and manage aphid vectors. Because nasturtium concentrates aphids, it can also serve as a virus reservoir, a reason to keep a trap stand at a distance from susceptible crops.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.note_beginner: In hot, humid regions a soilborne bacterial wilt can cause plants to suddenly droop and collapse. There is no cure; remove affected plants and avoid replanting in the same spot.
diseases.note_seasoned: Southern bacterial wilt (Ralstonia) can collapse plants in hot, humid soils, most relevant in the Deep South. No chemical control; remove infected plants and rotate away from the site. Uncommon outside warm humid regions.

diseases.name: Aster yellows
diseases.note_beginner: A disease spread by leafhoppers that yellows and distorts growth and can turn flowers green. There is no cure; remove and discard affected plants so it does not spread.
diseases.note_seasoned: A leafhopper-vectored phytoplasma causing chlorosis, distortion, and virescent blooms. No cure; rogue out symptomatic plants and manage leafhoppers and nearby weed reservoirs. Overall, nasturtium is bothered by few diseases.
